**Theorem.** Let $A$ be an Artinian ring and $M$ an $A$-module. Then $M$ is faithful if and only if there exists a natural number $r$ and an exact sequence $0 \to A \to M^{r}$.

**Proof.**

We prove both directions.

**($\Longleftarrow$) Exact sequence $\Rightarrow$ faithful.** This direction does not need the Artinian hypothesis. Suppose $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} M^{r}$ is exact, i.e. $f$ is injective. Since $A$ is cyclic (generated by $1$), $f$ is determined by $f(1)=(m_{1},\dots,m_{r})\in M^{r}$. For $a\in A$,
$$a\cdot f(1)=(am_{1},\dots,am_{r})=0 \iff a\in\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i}).$$
Injectivity of $f$ gives $\ker f=\operatorname{Ann}(f(1))=0$, hence
$$\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})=0.$$
Now $\operatorname{Ann}(M)=\bigcap_{m\in M}\operatorname{Ann}(m)\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})=0$, so $\operatorname{Ann}(M)=0$; $M$ is faithful.

**($\Longrightarrow$) Faithful $\Rightarrow$ exact sequence.** Here the Artinian hypothesis is essential. Assume $M$ is faithful, i.e. $\operatorname{Ann}(M)=\bigcap_{m\in M}\operatorname{Ann}(m)=0$. Consider the family of ideals
$$\mathcal{F}=\Bigl\{\,\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})\;:\;n\ge 1,\;m_{i}\in M\,\Bigr\}\subseteq\{\text{ideals of }A\}.$$
The family $\mathcal{F}$ is nonempty (it contains $\operatorname{Ann}(0)=A$). Since $A$ is Artinian, the set of all ideals of $A$ satisfies the descending chain condition, so every nonempty family of ideals has a minimal element. Let
$$I=\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})\in\mathcal{F}$$
be a minimal element of $\mathcal{F}$.

We claim $I=\operatorname{Ann}(M)=0$. For any $m\in M$, the ideal $I\cap\operatorname{Ann}(m)$ is again a finite intersection of annihilators of elements of $M$, so $I\cap\operatorname{Ann}(m)\in\mathcal{F}$, and $I\cap\operatorname{Ann}(m)\subseteq I$. By minimality of $I$ in $\mathcal{F}$,
$$I\cap\operatorname{Ann}(m)=I,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad I\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}(m).$$
This holds for every $m\in M$, so $I\subseteq\bigcap_{m\in M}\operatorname{Ann}(m)=\operatorname{Ann}(M)$. Conversely $\operatorname{Ann}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})$ for each $i$, hence $\operatorname{Ann}(M)\subseteq I$. Therefore
$$I=\operatorname{Ann}(M)=0.$$

Now define $f:A\to M^{r}$ by $f(a)=(am_{1},\dots,am_{r})$. This is an $A$-module homomorphism, and
$$\ker f=\{a\in A:am_{i}=0\;\forall i\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})=I=0.$$
Thus $f$ is injective, giving the exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{f}M^{r}$.

**Remark on the necessity of the Artinian hypothesis.** The converse direction genuinely uses the descending chain condition. For a non-Artinian counterexample, take $A=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}k$ (infinite product of a field $k$) and $M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\infty}k$ with coordinatewise action. Then $\operatorname{Ann}(M)=0$ (so $M$ is faithful), but for any finite set of elements $m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in M$, the intersection $\bigcap_{i}\operatorname{Ann}(m_{i})$ is a nonzero ideal (one can choose an element of $A$ vanishing on the finitely many coordinates supporting the $m_{i}$ and equal to $1$ elsewhere). Hence no injective map $A\to M^{r}$ exists. This confirms the Artinian assumption cannot be dropped. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
